basis.text: McIntosh's report of 4 August 1863 puts his brigade 'immediately engaged' after his move at 1 p.m.; Green's report of 8 July 1863 reads 2 p.m. (the second scan prints the digit; the first scan's is damaged); Rawle (1878) and Storrs (1889) put the first skirmish line and first shot at about two. The record of the time is divided by about an hour.

default.label: Between about 13:00 and 14:00; drawn at 14:00 (the latest hour a source gives for the start)
default.basis_text: Lower end: McIntosh (Union brigade commander, report of 4 August 1863): moved at 1 p.m. and was 'immediately engaged'. Upper end: Green (Confederate artillery, 8 July 1863: 2 p.m.; digit read from the second scan), Rawle (1878: McIntosh's skirmish line about two) and Storrs (1889, via Kidd: first shot not earlier than 2). Earlier contact on Custer's front (10:00, noon) and the main mounted clash (15:00) stay selectable.

animation.note: The fight is drawn from 14:00, the upper end of the window and the hour of Green, Rawle and Storrs; this is a drawing choice, not a settlement: McIntosh's report would put the engagement about an hour earlier, and no unit appears before its arrival.

default.note: The two best-class witnesses present, McIntosh (Union, 32 days) and Green (Confederate, 5 days), differ by about an hour; nothing in the rank rules separates them.

positions.label: About 13:00: McIntosh's brigade moves at 1 p.m. and is 'immediately engaged' (no hour for the first fire)

support.quote: I moved with my brigade at 1 p.m., July 3, 1863, to relieve Brigadier-General Custer's brigade [...] Hearing that the enemy were advancing from three directions, I immediately placed the First New Jersey Cavalry

witness.name: John B. McIntosh
witness.role: Colonel, Third Pennsylvania Cavalry, commanding the First Brigade, Second Division (Gregg's), on the field

support.note: McIntosh, a month after: he moved at 1 p.m. to relieve Custer; hearing the enemy were advancing he placed the First New Jersey at once and it was 'immediately engaged'. A move and an arrival, then the engagement, in one report; the report gives no hour for the first fire.

support.quote: When Mcintosh, with his command, came upon the ground shortly before one o'clock, for the purpose of relieving Custer

witness.name: William Brooke-Rawle
witness.role: Captain, Third Pennsylvania Cavalry, in McIntosh's brigade; wrote in 1878

support.note: Rawle: McIntosh reached the ground shortly before one o'clock. The same author puts the first skirmish line about two.
support.page_note: printed page 14 read from the text (15 begins a few lines later)

inference.step: McIntosh's own report says he moved at 1 p.m., placed the First New Jersey at once and that it 'became immediately engaged'; Rawle puts his arrival shortly before one. The engagement is read as soon after 13:00; Rawle, Green and Storrs put the first fire about an hour later.

support.quote: It was more than even their gallantry could stand, and the First Virginia fell back on the supports which were fast advancing to its assistance. This was about three o'clock

witness.name: William Brooke-Rawle
witness.role: Captain, Third Pennsylvania Cavalry, in McIntosh's brigade; wrote in 1878

support.note: Rawle: the First Virginia's attack was thrown back about three o'clock, as another brigade appeared at the Stallsmith farm, with Pickett then moving up to his assault. The hour of the main mounted clash, an hour after the fight began.
support.page_note: printed page 20 read from the text (21 begins after the next lines)

support.quote: According to the writer's diary this was about three o'clock

witness.name: William Brooke-Rawle
witness.role: Captain, Third Pennsylvania Cavalry; wrote the address in 1884 and cites his diary of 1863

support.note: Rawle's address of 1884, in a note to the same event: 'According to the writer's diary this was about three o'clock.' The diary itself is not in the library; this is the writer's statement of it.
support.page_note: printed page 22 read from the text (the page number follows the note)

reason_not_chosen.text: Rawle dates the charge and its repulse about three, an hour or more into the fight; it is not the start.

inference.step: Rawle says the First Virginia fell back about three o'clock after the fight had been hot for an hour; the hour of the clash is read as the plan's 15:00, not as the start.

positions.label: About noon: Pleasonton, Gregg's noon dispatch

support.quote: About noon the enemy threw a heavy force of cavalry against this position

witness.name: Alfred Pleasonton
witness.role: Major General commanding the Cavalry Corps (at corps headquarters; may relay Gregg, he does not say)

support.note: Pleasonton, nine weeks later, summarising: about noon the enemy threw a heavy force of cavalry against Gregg's position, an attack met and defeated by Gregg. He does not say how he knew the hour; Gregg's own report says the attack came after a noon dispatch.

support.quote: At 12 m. I received a copy of a dispatch from the commander of the Eleventh Army Corps to the major-general commanding the Army of the Potomac, that large columns of the enemy's cavalry were moving toward the right of our line

witness.name: David McM. Gregg
witness.role: Brigadier General, commanding the Second Cavalry Division, on the field

support.note: Gregg, three weeks after: at 12 m. he was handed the Eleventh Corps dispatch that large columns of Confederate cavalry were moving toward the right of the line; a strong line of skirmishers then showed that the cavalry had gained the right and was about to attack. The hour is the dispatch, not the first fire.

reason_not_chosen.text: Pleasonton gives an hour without saying how he knew (he may relay Gregg); Gregg's noon is the dispatch that warned him, with the attack still to come.

inference.step: Gregg received at 12 m. the warning that large columns of cavalry were moving to the right; Pleasonton, summarising, places the attack about noon. The first fire is read at or soon after the warning.

positions.label: 10:00: first contact on Custer's front (Custer's report, Fifth Michigan)

support.quote: Everything remained, quiet until 10 A. M., when the enemy appeared on my right flank and opened upon me with a battery of six guns

witness.name: George A. Custer
witness.role: Brigadier General, commanding the Michigan Cavalry Brigade (Second Brigade, Third Division) on the field; quoted from his report by Kidd in 1889

support.note: Custer's own report, as quoted by Kidd in 1889 (the report is not in the Official Records volume read here): quiet until 10 A.M., when the enemy appeared on his right flank and opened with a battery of six guns. The date of the report is not given in the quotation.
support.page_note: printed page 144 read from the running heads of the quoted passage (145 follows within the quotation)

support.quote: 3. — At 10 a. m. moved out, and met the enemy on the right, at Gettysburg

witness.name: George A. Custer (the Fifth Michigan Cavalry summary in his brigade report)
witness.role: Brigadier General commanding the Michigan Cavalry Brigade; the entry is for the Fifth Michigan Cavalry

support.note: The Fifth Michigan Cavalry's entry for July 3 in Custer's brigade report: 'At 10 a. m. moved out, and met the enemy on the right, at Gettysburg'. The same brigade, the same hour; the report heading in the text layer is garbled and the date of the whole report is given in the record only as September 1863.

reason_not_chosen.text: Both Michigan statements are from one brigade; Storrs, of the same brigade, and Rawle put the first shot at 2, and Green dates the engagement 2 p.m.

inference.step: Custer says quiet until 10 A.M. when a battery opened on his right flank; read as the first contact of the day, which Rawle and Kidd doubt (Kidd suggests the copied report misread 1 o'clock as 10).

positions.label: About 14:00: the engagement begins (Green: 2 p.m.; McIntosh's skirmish line about two)

support.quote: commenced at 'Z p. m. by the dismounted sharp- shooters

witness.name: C. A. Green
witness.role: Captain, Louisiana Guard Artillery, commanding a section of two Parrott guns with Hampton's brigade

support.note: Green, five days after, with his guns on the field: 'The engagement commenced at 2 p. m. by the dismounted sharpshooters on both sides.' The text layer of the first scan prints a letter, 'Z', for the digit; the text layer of the second scan of the same volume (SCAN2-C005, unproofread, no page marks) prints 2: 'The engagement commenced at 2 p. m. by the dismounted sharp-'. The page image could not be fetched, so the digit rests on the two text layers and is flagged. His report does not name the day in this sentence; it follows 'Thursday evening, July 2' and 'until morning', and precedes 'Saturday evening, July 4'.

support.quote: Accordingly, about two o'clock he ordered Major Beaumont to deploy a strong skirmish line of the First New Jersey, and move it forward [...] This movement was a signal for the deployment of a skirmish line from Rummel's barn

witness.name: William Brooke-Rawle
witness.role: Captain, Third Pennsylvania Cavalry, in McIntosh's brigade (author of the pamphlet); wrote in 1878

support.note: Rawle, 15 years later: McIntosh, waiting after relieving Custer, ordered a strong skirmish line of the First New Jersey forward about two o'clock; this drew out the Confederate skirmish line from the Rummel barn and the fight began.
support.page_note: printed page 17 read from the text (the page number 17 stands inside the preceding sentence)

support.quote: He states that the first shot was not fired till some time after his recall, and he is sure it was not earlier than 2 o'clock

witness.name: Charles E. Storrs
witness.role: Major, 6th Michigan Cavalry, commanding a squadron sent out in front of Custer's position (reported by Kidd in 1889)

support.note: Storrs, a squadron commander of Custer's brigade, as given by Kidd in his address of 12 June 1889: recalled about noon (he is sure later than 12 m.), the first shot not fired until some time after, 'not earlier than 2 o'clock'. A recollection of 26 years, relayed by Kidd; a lower bound.
support.page_note: printed page 147 of Michigan at Gettysburg read from the running heads (146 and 148 stand before and after)

support.quote: it was 2 o’clock before the forces were seriously engaged

witness.name: unnamed author of the New York volume (a history)
witness.role: Chapter of New York at Gettysburg (1900), not a participant

support.note: A history of 1900: Fitz Lee's and Hampton's brigades reached the field about 11 o'clock and their artillery opened on Custer, 'but it was 2 o'clock before the forces were seriously engaged'. No source named.
support.page_note: no printed page marks in the text layer; the passage is in the chapter on the cavalry fight of July 3

inference.step: Green (Confederate, July 1863) dates the engagement at 2 p.m. in a report that runs from July 2 to 4; Rawle and Storrs, of the Union side, put the first shot and the first skirmish line at about two. The day is read from the order of Green's report. Storrs gives only a lower bound ('not earlier than 2'); the history of 1900 names no source and is not counted among the independent groups.

weighing.summary: The two best-class witnesses present disagree: McIntosh (official report, 32 days after) has his brigade 'immediately engaged' after the 1 p.m. move; Green (official report, 5 days after, Confederate) has the engagement begin at 2 p.m., the digit read from the second scan. Rawle (1878) and Storrs (via Kidd, 1889) put the first skirmish line and first shot at about two. Noon is Gregg's warning, 15:00 the main mounted clash, 10:00 Custer's early contact. Nothing in the rank rules separates McIntosh from Green (Green is nearer in time, McIntosh is on the Union side where the clash began), so the record is divided and the window is shown.
weighing.who: Green fired a Confederate section in the fight; McIntosh and Gregg commanded on the Union side; Pleasonton was at corps headquarters; Custer commanded the brigade on the field; Rawle and Storrs were officers in the fight and wrote or spoke years later (1878, 1889). Stuart's report gives no hour; the reports of Fitz Lee, Chambliss, Ferguson and W. H. F. Lee are not printed.
weighing.when: Green wrote 5 days after, Gregg 22, McIntosh 32, Pleasonton 59 days after; Rawle 15 years and Storrs 26 years after. The best class of writing (reports of the time) gives Green 2 p.m., McIntosh 1 p.m. as a move, Gregg noon as a dispatch, Pleasonton about noon as a relay; the later participants Rawle and Storrs agree with Green.
weighing.where: Green's guns were on the Confederate side near the Rummel buildings; McIntosh was with the First New Jersey on the Union right; Storrs was in front of Custer's position; Gregg was at the right of the line. They saw different parts of a front half a mile wide, and the Confederate artillery and skirmishers may have opened earlier on Custer's front than the main engagement.
weighing.how_knew: Green gives a clock reading from the field; McIntosh gives the hour of his own move; Gregg the hour of a dispatch handed to him; Rawle and Storrs recall hours across many years, Rawle partly from a diary.
weighing.clock: Green uses the Confederate clock, the Union writers the Union clock; the reported difference of about 20 minutes is not applied and is too small to join noon and 14:00.
weighing.independence: Green (Confederate) is independent of the Union writers. McIntosh and Rawle are of one brigade, but Rawle's account of 1878 and McIntosh's report disagree on the hour. Storrs's statement reaches us through Kidd, who wrote knowing Rawle's pamphlet, so Storrs and Rawle may not be independent of each other. The NY-GB history (1900) names no source and is not counted. Storrs gives only a lower bound ('not earlier than 2'). Pleasonton may relay Gregg; he does not say. Counted for about two: Green, Rawle, Storrs (lower bound); for about 13:00: McIntosh; one group each for noon, 10:00 and 15:00.

source_panel_text: Between about 13:00 and 14:00 on Jul 3; drawn at 14:00. McIntosh's report says his brigade was engaged at once after moving at 1 p.m.; Green (Confederate artillery) reads 2 p.m. (second scan; the first scan's digit is damaged), and Rawle and Storrs say about two. Noon, 10:00 and 15:00 date other events. Three other values are listed.
